description: AeroMedPack veri toplayan, kutudaki yerel AI ile anlık analiz yapıp iletişim kopsa dahi uyarı veren ve ana üsse senkronize olan giyilebilir otonom erken uyarı sistemidir. 3 aşamalı çalışır: Veri toplama, yerel yapay zeka analizi ve merkez senkronizasyonu. "Biyolojik kara kutu" özelliği sayesinde 30 günlük veriyi güvenle saklayarak olası kazaların saniyeler içinde incelenmesini sağlar. Astronot sağlığı için kritik bir güvencedir.
summary:
AeroMedPack is a software prototype for astronaut health monitoring that keeps working when the communication link does not. It runs in the browser with synthetic data and simulates a chest-worn sensor hub that logs heart rate, skin temperature and an ECG-like signal (plus experimental SpO₂ and respiration estimates).

Every record is stored locally first, queued during an outage, then sent with acknowledgements when contact returns; duplicates are rejected. The Earth-side dashboard shows only what was actually received and labels data as STALE with its age. Health screening uses transparent, explainable rules, and link or sensor problems raise separate technical alerts, so an outage is never mistaken for a medical emergency.

This matters because on the ISS delay is short, but on Mars-class missions one-way delay reaches about 22 minutes and solar conjunction can cut contact for roughly two weeks. The prototype does not diagnose, uses simulated data and is not a medical device; six acceptance tests (T1–T6) show what works.
details:
What it does and how it works
AeroMedPack is a browser-based prototype of astronaut health-monitoring software built around one idea: records must never be silently lost when the link drops, and Earth must always see how fresh the data really is. A simulated wearable generates synthetic heart rate, skin temperature, ECG-like waveform and experimental SpO₂ and respiration values. Each sample gets a unique ID, a timestamp and a quality flag and is written to a local queue (IndexedDB) that survives a page reload. A simulated station gateway receives records in batches, returns acknowledgements and rejects duplicate IDs. Unacknowledged records stay queued and are resent when contact returns, with their original timestamps. The Earth-side view shows only what was actually received and marks data STALE, with its age, after a 5-second freshness window.

Health screening uses transparent, rolling-baseline rules, and every flag carries a “why”. Link loss, stale data and sensor faults raise a separate technical alert, so an outage is never presented as a medical emergency. The live demo lets you cut the link, add packet loss, inject scenarios (elevated heart rate, temperature rise, low SpO₂, sensor fault) and replay a duplicate. Six acceptance tests (T1–T6) tick off as you exercise it.

Benefits and intended impact
On the ISS, delay is short and Earth-based flight surgeons can review data. On Mars-class missions, one-way delay reaches about 22 minutes and solar conjunction can cut contact for roughly two weeks. The intended impact is a small, testable application layer that keeps data intact, labels its age honestly and keeps health and technical alerts apart, so crews and ground teams are not misled by missing or old data.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no backend); IndexedDB for the local queue; Three.js for the 3D device concept; SVG and canvas for waveforms and charts; a bilingual (Turkish/English) interface; a 46-second concept animation and a 9-page technical brief (PDF). [List the tools you used for the video and PDF.] No real hardware was built: the device, sensors, radio and the “Earth server” are simulated or concept drawings and are labeled that way. [Add an AI-assistance statement if the challenge requires one.]

Creativity
The prototype turns honesty into a feature: a visible “Honest Status” section separates what works from what is only concept, and the interface labels every value as simulated. Interactive labs make the problem tangible: a Communication Delay Lab (ISS, Moon, Mars, solar conjunction), an Alert Workshop with sliders and a “Health or Technical?” quiz.

Factors the team considered

  • Non-clinical scope: the system supports situational awareness, does not diagnose and is not a medical device.
  • Skin temperature is not core temperature, and microgravity removes natural convection, so heat must spread by conduction.
  • Radio placement on the body, planning estimates for power (≤50 mW average) and storage (about 2.8 MB per day of records), all labeled as assumptions, not measurements.
  • Privacy: public demos use synthetic data only.
  • Limitations: no real hardware yet, rule-based screening instead of a trained model, simulated server.
dataRefs: NASA RFI: Practical Ways to Monitor Astronaut Body Temperature in Low Earth Orbit
